claim: Confident AI's internal data across 250k+ annotated test cases each shows single-output G-Eval judges align with human review 95.1% of the time and pairwise Arena G-Eval judges align 94.6% of the time, both exceeding typical human-to-human inter-annotator agreement (~81%).
stance_target: pillar 1: rigid evals — LLM-as-judge reliability baseline
scope_conditions: Confident AI customer data (thumbs up/down annotations), 250k+ test cases per method, 2026
quoted_support: Single-output and pairwise judges both align with 95% of human reviews... 95.1% ... 94.6% ... Alignment rate with human annotation.

claim: Published research shows GPT-4 as an LLM judge reaches up to ~85% agreement with human annotators, which exceeds the ~81% agreement rate between two human annotators on the same task.
stance_target: pillar 1: LLM-as-judge viability as replacement for human eval at scale
scope_conditions: cited from the MT-Bench/Chatbot Arena research line
quoted_support: state-of-the-art LLMs such as GPT-4 (yes, still GPT-4) have the ability to align with human judgement to up to 85%, for both pairwise and single-output scoring... this number is actually even higher than the agreement among humans (81%).

claim: LLM judges exhibit narcissistic/self-favoring bias: cited research found GPT-4 favors its own outputs with a 10% higher win rate and Claude-v1 favors its own outputs with a 25% higher win rate, while GPT-3.5 does not favor itself.
stance_target: assumption that an LLM judge is a neutral arbiter of its own or peer model outputs
scope_conditions: cited prior research on model self-preference in pairwise judging
quoted_support: research has shown that although GPT-4 and Claude-v1 favors itself with a 10% and 25% higher win rate respectively, they also favor other models and GPT-3.5 does not favor itself.

claim: Few-shot prompting increases GPT-4 LLM-judge scoring consistency from 65.0% to 77.5%.
stance_target: pillar 1: concrete mitigation technique for rigid, reproducible LLM-as-judge evals
scope_conditions: cited study on few-shot prompting effect on judge consistency
quoted_support: few-shot prompting has shown to increase GPT-4's consistency from 65.0% to 77.5%.

claim: DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) decision-tree evaluation structures, where nodes are LLM judges and edges represent branching decisions, achieve deterministic scoring for criteria with a clear right answer (e.g., format correctness), unlike G-Eval which remains non-deterministic and better suited to genuinely subjective criteria.
stance_target: pillar 1: rigid, reproducible evals requiring deterministic decomposition of LLM judgment
quoted_support: There's a problem with G-Eval though, because it is not deterministic... You can achieve this with LLMs by structuring evaluations as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). In this approach, each node represents an LLM judge handling a specific decision, while edges define the logical flow between decisions.

claim: LLM judges exhibit position bias in pairwise comparisons (GPT-4 generally prefers the first-shown output) and verbosity bias (judges tend to prefer more verbose text over concise text regardless of actual quality).
stance_target: assumption that pairwise LLM-judge comparisons are order-independent and quality-calibrated
quoted_support: When using LLM judges for pairwise comparisons, it has been shown that LLMs such as GPT-4 generally prefer the first generated LLM output over the second one... LLM judges tend to prefer more verbose text over more concise ones.

claim: QAG (question-answer-generation) decomposes subjective LLM judgments into yes/no answers to close-ended sub-questions, making metric scores attributable to a mathematical formula rather than arbitrary and reducing hallucination risk because less text is analyzed per judgment.
stance_target: pillar 1: decomposition technique to reduce LLM-judge arbitrariness and hallucination
scope_conditions: DeepEval QAG-based metrics (answer relevancy, contextual precision)
quoted_support: QAG is a powerful technique because it means LLM scores are no longer arbitrary and can be attributed to a mathematical formula. Breaking down the initial prompt to only include sentences instead of the entire LLM output can also help combat hallucinations as there is now less text to be analyzed.
